Conversely, from any tuple x in K_{m,g}, define S(x) by including 0, all positive multiples of m, and in residue class r all numbers qm+r with q >= x_r. The stated inequalities are exactly what is needed to check closure under addition; positivity of x_r gives multiplicity m; the coordinate sum gives genus g. The two constructions are inverse, so N(m,g)=|K_{m,g}|.

The proof gives a standard and complete bijection between numerical semigroups of multiplicity m and genus g and Kunz-coordinate tuples in K_{m,g}. It correctly constructs the forward map via the least element in each nonzero residue class modulo m, verifies positivity, the two inequality families, and the genus sum formula. It then defines the inverse set S(x), proves finite complement, multiplicity m, closure under addition by exhaustive residue-class analysis, and computes the genus. Finally it proves both compositions are identities. The argument matches the semantic sketch exactly and is well aligned with the root theorem’s counting interpretation.

For (b)=> (a), one checks closure of S_x under addition by cases on residues i+j<m, i+j=m, i+j>m, using the stated inequalities to rewrite sums as either a multiple of m or a nonnegative multiple of m plus the appropriate w_k. Cofiniteness follows because every n>=max_i w_i lies in S_x by residue-class reduction, and m is the least positive element since all w_i>m. For (a)=> (b), closure gives w_i+w_j in S_x; comparing its residue modulo m with the explicit description of S_x forces w_i+w_j=t m+w_k, yielding the inequalities. For an arbitrary numerical semigroup S of multiplicity m, least representatives w_i in each nonzero residue class exist by cofiniteness, satisfy w_i=m x_i+i with x_i>=1 (else there would be a positive element <m in S), the same inequalities follow from minimality of the w_i, and every element of S is either a multiple of m or equals q m+w_i for the appropriate residue, giving the reconstruction formula.

The proof establishes both directions of the equivalence and the moreover clause in a mathematically complete way. The closure argument for S_x handles all residue cases, finite complement is proved by a standard conductor-style bound using M = max w_i, multiplicity m is justified from x_i >= 1, and the converse derives the Kunz inequalities from closure and residue considerations. The moreover clause correctly proves existence/minimality of the Apéry representatives w_i, positivity of x_i, the inequalities, and reconstruction of S from residue-class minima. The argument matches the semantic sketch with no material drift.

I was able to verify some useful structural facts about the sets K_{m,g}, but I could not complete a rigorous proof of the required injective map. In particular, I showed: (1) if x in K_{m,g} and x_k is a minimum coordinate of x, then x+e_k lies in K_{m,g+1}; and (2) if y in K_{m,g+1} and y_k is a maximum coordinate with y_k>1, then y-e_k lies in K_{m,g}. These facts suggest an upward/downward adjacency between consecutive genus layers, but I could not turn them into a full injection or into a surjection in the opposite direction satisfying Hall-type conditions. I also checked that naive canonical choices fail: for m=3, the tuples (1,2) and (2,1) in K_{3,3} each have only one obvious '+1 to a minimum coordinate' extension, and both lead to (2,2), so that simple map is not injective.

I could verify that a natural map exists at the level of membership preservation: if x\in K_{m,g} and t is an index where x_t is minimal, then increasing x_t by 1 keeps all defining inequalities valid, because every coordinate is at least x_t and positive. However, I could not turn this into an injective map. The obvious tie-breakings (leftmost minimal coordinate or rightmost minimal coordinate) are not injective: for m=4, both x=(1,2,1) and x'=(2,1,1) are valid elements of K_{4,4}, and leftmost-minimum increment sends them both to (2,2,1); similarly rightmost-minimum increment sends (1,1,2) and (1,2,1) to (1,2,2). I do not currently have a rigorous construction of an injective J_{m,g}, nor a self-contained counting argument proving |K_{m,g}|\le |K_{m,g+1}| for all m,g.

I could not complete a rigorous proof of the existence of an injective map J_{m,g}: K_{m,g} -> K_{m,g+1} from the tuple inequalities alone. I found a plausible partial idea: if k is an index where x_k is minimal among the coordinates of x, then x+e_k always still satisfies the defining inequalities, so every x in K_{m,g} has at least one 'incrementable' coordinate. However, the obvious deterministic choices (such as incrementing the first minimal coordinate, last minimal coordinate, smallest incrementable coordinate, etc.) can collide, and I was not able to construct a collision-free canonical rule or another cardinality argument that is justified solely from the given self-contained definition of K_{m,g}.
